saints.name: Cher Horowitz + Dionne Davenport
saints.about: A LAiDIES teaching duo inspired by two fictional friends who make taste practical, social, and unmistakably their own.
saints.lesson: Build a useful, personal way of working that other people want to copy. Trendsetting creates the pattern; staying current notices what changed.
saints.songLabel: Cher's song · duo version to come
saints.whyHere: Cher Horowitz and Dionne Davenport are here because trendsetting is not simply being first to try a new thing. It is turning one useful, distinctive experiment into a pattern another person can recognise, test, and adapt without becoming a copy of you.
contribution: This is a LAiDIES teaching duo inspired by two fictional friends whose coordinated looks remain unmistakably individual; that distinction is the teaching clue.
Their role is trendsetting: make a useful pattern visible enough to travel, then let another person adapt it with her own judgment.
saints.move: Start with a recurring problem, define what better would mean, make the input, AI job, and human checks visible, then let someone else adapt the method. A pattern that works only while its inventor supervises every step is a performance, not a practice. Trendsetting creates the pattern; staying current notices what has changed.
saints.tryIt: Choose one repeated task, such as assembling a weekly project update. Record how long it takes now and the mistake you most want to prevent. Test an AI-assisted first draft using only approved notes, then check every name, date, commitment, and unresolved risk against the sources. Give the resulting four-part recipe—allowed input, AI job, human check, and success measure—to one colleague and ask what still works after she adapts it.
saints.boundary: Popularity is not proof: a widely copied workflow can still be inaccurate, unsafe, or wrong for another person's work. This is a LAiDIES interpretation of fictional characters, not a biography, endorsement, or quotation.

concepts.name: Workflow design
concepts.connection: A repeatable AI practice needs a visible sequence of inputs, tool actions and human checks—not one lucky prompt.

concepts.name: Adoption and diffusion
concepts.connection: A method spreads when another person can understand it, adapt it and still produce a useful result.

concepts.name: Human judgement
concepts.connection: The originator decides what makes the pattern worth copying; popularity cannot make a weak process sound.

saints.humanInteraction: People do not interact with AI only by typing requests. They also design the surrounding routine: what material is allowed in, what the tool produces, who checks it and how another person can reuse it. Cher and Dionne make the distinction between copying a look and learning the logic that makes it work.
saints.whyItMattersNow: Teams are rapidly turning personal AI experiments into shared workflows. If the method cannot survive handoff, adaptation and review, the organisation has not adopted a practice—it has become dependent on one person's improvisation.

saints.name: David Rose
saints.about: A LAiDIES teaching device inspired by a fictional curator with exacting taste and very little patience for vague.
saints.lesson: Name the outcome, audience, constraints, and taste before asking AI to make anything.
saints.whyHere: David Rose is here because vague requests produce vague work. His role is to make the reader name what she actually wants before inviting AI to make it.
contribution: This is a LAiDIES teaching device inspired by a fictional curator with exacting taste and very little patience for vague.
His lesson is specificity: name the outcome, audience, constraints, and taste before asking AI to make anything.
saints.move: Specificity is not piling adjectives onto a prompt. It is deciding the job: who this is for, what it must achieve, what material it may use, and what would make the result unusable. Those decisions give you a way to judge a draft rather than merely react to it.
saints.tryIt: Take one request you would normally type in one sentence. Rewrite it with four headings: audience, outcome, source material, and non-negotiable constraint. Ask AI for a first draft, then check it against each heading before changing its style. If you cannot explain why a detail belongs, remove it rather than treating the prompt as a mood board.
saints.boundary: A precise request cannot rescue weak source material or replace a human decision about quality. It only makes the target and the gaps easier to see.

concepts.name: Prompt and requirements design
concepts.connection: Making the outcome, audience, evidence and constraints visible makes an AI result more controllable and reviewable instead of leaving important choices to the model's guesses.

concepts.name: Context
concepts.connection: Relevant background changes which answer is useful; decorative detail does not substitute for task information.

concepts.name: Evaluation criteria
concepts.connection: Specific instructions give the reviewer something concrete to compare with the result.

saints.humanInteraction: When people use generative AI, they are commissioning a draft. They shape the result by specifying the job, supplying relevant context and naming what must not change. The interaction continues when they compare the output with those requirements.
saints.whyItMattersNow: Vague AI requests often create polished but interchangeable work. In a workplace, specificity reduces avoidable revision, exposes missing decisions early and makes quality less dependent on whether the tool happened to guess the user's taste.

saints.name: Elle Woods
saints.about: A LAiDIES teaching device inspired by a fictional lawyer who refuses to let other people's assumptions do the reasoning.
saints.lesson: Test the evidence, assumptions, and logic before deciding whether an AI answer actually holds.
saints.whyHere: Elle Woods is here because an AI answer does not become sound reasoning merely by arriving in a confident tone. Her role is critical thinking: test the evidence, assumptions, and logic before you rely on a conclusion.
contribution: This is a LAiDIES teaching device inspired by a fictional lawyer who refuses to let other people's assumptions do the reasoning.
Her lesson is to test whether an AI answer actually holds, rather than mistaking polish, confidence, or familiarity for proof.
saints.move: Separate a conclusion from the steps that are supposed to support it. Ask what claim is being made, what evidence would count, which assumption links them, and what fact would change the answer. That turns critical thinking into a repeatable check instead of a decorative warning to be careful.
saints.tryIt: Choose one AI answer that recommends a decision. Write its conclusion, the evidence it relies on, and the assumption that is supposed to connect the two. Then look for one plausible counterexample or missing fact that would break that inference. If the recommendation no longer follows, revise the reasoning or keep the answer as a starting question rather than the decision itself.
saints.boundary: Critical thinking is not automatic suspicion or endless debate. It is proportionate checking: the more a wrong answer could cost, the stronger the evidence and human review should be.

concepts.name: Evaluation
concepts.connection: An answer is tested against evidence and success criteria rather than accepted because it sounds plausible.

concepts.name: Hallucination and grounding
concepts.connection: Generated claims need a traceable connection to the documents, data or observations that could support them.

concepts.name: Reasoning under uncertainty
concepts.connection: The reviewer separates what is established, inferred and still unknown before making a decision.

saints.humanInteraction: A person supplies the standard of proof that the model cannot supply for itself. She checks whether cited material exists, whether it supports the exact conclusion and whether the reasoning skipped a decisive fact. Follow-up prompts can help investigate, but they do not replace independent verification.
saints.whyItMattersNow: AI is increasingly used to summarise research, policies, contracts and business information. A confident error can travel directly into a presentation or decision unless someone treats the output as a claim to examine rather than a verdict to repeat.

saints.name: Samantha Jones
saints.about: A LAiDIES teaching device inspired by a fictional publicist who reads the room and chooses the approach that can do the job.
saints.lesson: Choose the right model, tool, or mode for the work instead of asking one chatbot to be everything.
saints.whyHere: Samantha Jones is here because one chatbot should not be asked to be every tool for every job. Her role is tool choice: read the room, identify the work, and choose the approach that can actually do it.
contribution: This is a LAiDIES teaching device inspired by a fictional publicist who reads the room and chooses the approach that can do the job.
Her lesson is to choose the right model, tool, or mode for the work instead of treating one familiar chatbot as the universal answer.
saints.move: Begin with the job's real shape: drafting, finding evidence, analysing a file, making an image, or turning speech into notes are not the same task. Then ask what input the tool needs, what output it can actually produce, and where a person must check it. Choosing a tool becomes a work decision, not a loyalty test.
saints.tryIt: Take one task you have been giving to the same AI tool by habit. Write down the input, the output you need, the privacy level, and the check that matters. Compare two suitable approaches only on that job, using the same small test material. Keep the one that produces the more usable result with the safer and clearer handoff, not the flashier demo.
saints.boundary: The newest or most famous tool is not automatically the right one. Tool choice also cannot remove responsibility for the final work.

concepts.name: Model and tool selection
concepts.connection: Different systems have different strengths, limits, data access and risk profiles.

concepts.name: Modality
concepts.connection: Text, image, audio, video, code and data tasks require different ways of representing and checking information.

concepts.name: Affordances
concepts.connection: The right interface makes the intended action easier and the dangerous action harder.

saints.humanInteraction: People choose not just what to ask, but which system should receive the task. They decide whether the job needs live information, private-file handling, image generation, calculation, coding or simple drafting, then review the result using checks appropriate to that medium.
saints.whyItMattersNow: Using one chatbot for every job can create unnecessary privacy, accuracy and quality problems. Good tool choice saves time only when the selection accounts for the real task, the sensitivity of the material and the form the finished work must take.

saints.name: Miranda Priestly
saints.about: A LAiDIES teaching device inspired by a fictional editor whose first question is whether the work is actually good enough.
saints.lesson: Treat the first output as a draft. Inspect it, name the gap, and require another pass.
saints.whyHere: Miranda Priestly is here because a first output is a draft, not a verdict. Her role is standards: inspect the work, name the gap, and require another pass when the result does not meet the job.
contribution: This is a LAiDIES teaching device inspired by a fictional editor whose first question is whether the work is actually good enough.
Her lesson treats AI output as something to review against a stated standard, not something to accept because it appeared quickly.
saints.move: Set the standard before you see the output, or the output will quietly set the standard for you. Name the few conditions that make the work ready—perhaps correct facts, a clear audience fit, no confidential material, and a usable next step. Review against those conditions, then give a specific revision instruction rather than saying 'make it better'.
saints.tryIt: Before generating a draft, write three acceptance checks for it. When it arrives, mark each check pass, fail, or unclear and quote the exact line that caused the judgment. Ask for one revision tied to the failed check, then compare the new version with the old one. Stop after the draft meets the actual job; do not keep revising merely because AI makes another pass easy.
saints.boundary: High standards are not the same as endless perfectionism. A standard should be tied to the purpose and consequence of the work, not to an impossible ideal.

concepts.name: Human feedback
concepts.connection: A model's first output becomes useful through specific correction, comparison and another pass.

concepts.name: Evaluation rubrics
concepts.connection: Quality improves when standards are observable rather than reduced to 'make it better.'

concepts.name: Iteration
concepts.connection: Revision is a controlled loop, not endless regeneration with no record of what changed.

saints.humanInteraction: The person remains the editor. She identifies the most consequential gap, states the required correction and checks whether the next version actually solved it without damaging something that already worked. The AI supplies alternatives; the human owns the standard.
saints.whyItMattersNow: Generative systems make first drafts cheap, which can tempt teams to lower the bar or produce endless versions. Explicit standards turn speed into useful progress and stop fluent mediocrity from becoming the default simply because it arrived quickly.

saints.name: Deb
saints.about: LAiDIES' own keeper of the line between helpful delegation and information or authority that should stay human.
saints.lesson: Decide what AI should not receive, decide, or do before you begin.
saints.whyHere: Deb is here because the useful question is not only what AI can do, but what it should never receive, decide, or do. Her role is boundaries: keep authority and information on the human side when the work calls for it.
contribution: Deb is LAiDIES' own keeper of the line between helpful delegation and information or authority that should stay human.
Her lesson asks the reader to decide the boundary before she begins, instead of discovering it after private information or decision-making power has already crossed it.
saints.move: Draw three lines before you use a tool: what may go in, what AI may draft or organise, and what a person must decide. A boundary is useful when it changes the workflow, not when it sits in a policy document nobody consults. Clear handoffs keep convenience from quietly becoming delegation of authority.
saints.tryIt: Choose one AI workflow and make a three-column note: allowed input, prohibited input, and human-only decisions. Test the workflow with a harmless sample rather than a live sensitive case. Ask the person accountable for the decision to confirm the last column. If there is no named human owner, the workflow is not ready for that decision.
saints.boundary: A boundary is not a promise that all risk has disappeared. It needs review when the task, tool, data, or consequence changes.

concepts.name: Data governance
concepts.connection: People decide what information a system may receive, retain and pass to another service.

concepts.name: Automation boundaries
concepts.connection: Some actions may be drafted by AI but must remain human decisions or require approval.

concepts.name: Privacy and security
concepts.connection: Risk depends on the data, provider, permissions and downstream use—not only the wording of the prompt.

saints.humanInteraction: Before opening a tool, a person sets the boundary: which files are permitted, which facts are confidential, which decisions cannot be delegated and who may see the output. Refusing an unsafe input or action is part of competent AI use, not a failure to innovate.
saints.whyItMattersNow: Workplace AI often sits one copy-and-paste away from customer records, employee information, contracts and internal strategy. A boundary established after disclosure is too late; teams need rules that operate before convenience takes over.

saints.name: Buffy Summers
saints.about: A LAiDIES teaching device inspired by a fictional heroine who can carry the stakes and still finish tonight's actual job.
saints.lesson: Stop dabbling. Define one bounded whole job, use AI where it helps, and finish it.
saints.whyHere: Buffy Summers is here because exploration has to end in a finished piece of work. Her role is execution: define one bounded whole job, use AI where it helps, and finish it tonight rather than collecting endless experiments.
contribution: This is a LAiDIES teaching device inspired by a fictional heroine who can carry the stakes and still finish tonight's actual job.
Her lesson is to stop dabbling by choosing a complete, bounded task with a clear definition of done.
saints.move: Turn an interesting possibility into a finite job with a beginning, an output, a check, and a finish line. Use AI at the point where it removes real friction, then return to the human check that makes the work safe to send or use. Completion creates evidence about whether the tool helped; endless prompting does not.
saints.tryIt: Pick one task that can be completed in a single work session, such as turning approved notes into a one-page brief. Define the output, the time limit, and the person who will check it. Use AI for one named subtask only, then finish the brief and run the check before the time ends. Write down whether AI reduced a real obstacle or merely added another activity.
saints.boundary: Not every job should be rushed or reduced to a one-session sprint. The point is to finish a bounded test, not to treat speed as the only value.

concepts.name: Task decomposition
concepts.connection: A large job becomes manageable when its inputs, stages, dependencies and checks are made explicit.

concepts.name: AI workflows and agents
concepts.connection: A system may perform several connected actions, but each action still needs permissions and an observable completion condition.

concepts.name: Human oversight
concepts.connection: The accountable person watches the consequential transitions rather than approving a finished bundle blindly.

saints.humanInteraction: People move from casual prompting to execution by defining a bounded result, assigning the portions AI can handle and retaining review at the points where an error would compound. The job is not finished when the model stops talking; it is finished when the real deliverable has been checked and used.
saints.whyItMattersNow: AI products increasingly promise multi-step work, from research through drafting and action. Clear scope and checkpoints prevent a small early mistake from spreading through the whole chain while still allowing automation to reduce genuinely repetitive effort.

saints.name: Dolly Parton
saints.about: A playful LAiDIES teaching tribute to plain judgment, warmth, and knowing when clever has become unnecessarily complicated.
saints.lesson: Use common sense as a quality check. If the elaborate answer makes the real job harder, simplify it.
saints.whyHere: Dolly Parton is here because clever can become unnecessarily complicated. Her role is common sense: if an elaborate answer makes the real job harder, simplify it.
contribution: This is a playful LAiDIES teaching tribute to plain judgment, warmth, and knowing when clever has become unnecessarily complicated.
Her lesson makes common sense a quality check for AI work rather than a vague preference for whatever feels easy.
saints.move: Ask what a sensible person needs to do next after reading or using the output. If a summary obscures the decision, an image hides the message, or a workflow adds more checking than it saves, the extra cleverness is not serving the job. Simplifying is a test of usefulness, not a failure of ambition.
saints.tryIt: Take one AI output you have already revised several times. Ask a colleague who was not involved to explain the decision, action, or message it is meant to support. Check what she misses or misunderstands, then remove one layer of detail, decoration, or process that did not help. Keep the simpler version only if it makes the next action clearer without losing an essential fact.
saints.boundary: Simple is not the same as simplistic. Some decisions genuinely require detail, evidence, and careful explanation. This is a LAiDIES teaching tribute, not a biography, endorsement, or claim about Dolly Parton’s views on AI.

concepts.name: Decision usefulness
concepts.connection: An AI output is valuable only when it helps a person understand, decide or act.

concepts.name: Complexity and simplification
concepts.connection: More detail, tools or steps can reduce quality when they obscure the actual job.

concepts.name: Automation bias
concepts.connection: People may overvalue an elaborate machine-produced answer even when ordinary judgement reveals it is impractical.

saints.humanInteraction: A person compares the AI's proposal with the real situation: the available time, the people affected, the cost of the process and the decision that must be made. She can ask for a simpler version, remove unnecessary machinery or reject the output altogether.
saints.whyItMattersNow: AI makes it easy to generate plans, frameworks and analysis that look more sophisticated than the problem requires. Common sense protects teams from spending more effort managing the AI solution than solving the original problem.

saints.name: Sister Mary Clarence
saints.about: A LAiDIES teaching device inspired by a fictional teacher who makes the whole room stronger instead of performing expertise at it.
saints.lesson: Explain the method, not just the answer, so someone else can use it without you.
saints.whyHere: Sister Mary Clarence is here because a useful method should make the whole room stronger, not leave everyone dependent on the person who discovered it. Her role is teaching: explain the method, not just the answer.
contribution: This is a LAiDIES teaching device inspired by a fictional teacher who makes the whole room stronger instead of performing expertise at it.
Her lesson is to show another person how to use a method without you, rather than handing over an answer with its reasoning hidden.
saints.move: Teach the repeatable parts: the starting material, the tool's limited job, the human check, and the sign that the method has failed. That gives another person enough structure to adapt the practice without pretending every situation is identical. The method becomes more useful when it can be explained back.
saints.tryIt: Choose one AI workflow you have figured out for yourself. Write a short guide that includes one input example, one prompt or instruction pattern, one check, and one common failure. Ask a colleague to use it on a related task without you in the room. Revise the guide based on what she could not understand or safely decide.
saints.boundary: A reusable guide cannot replace judgment, context, or training for high-consequence work. Its job is to make the method visible, not to automate teaching away.

concepts.name: Explainability
concepts.connection: A useful explanation shows the steps and evidence needed to understand a result, not merely a confident conclusion.

concepts.name: Knowledge transfer
concepts.connection: A method becomes organisational knowledge when another person can use and adapt it.

concepts.name: Human-in-the-loop learning
concepts.connection: People improve both the output and their own judgement by questioning, correcting and explaining the process.

saints.humanInteraction: Instead of asking AI to provide an answer for someone else, the user asks it to reveal the method, check understanding and create a new example. The learner then explains the idea back and tests it in a different situation, exposing whether understanding actually transferred.
saints.whyItMattersNow: Workplaces can use AI either to hide thinking or to spread capability. Teaching the method reduces dependence on one expert or one tool and helps colleagues recognise when a future answer does not fit the situation.

saints.name: Carrie Bradshaw
saints.about: A LAiDIES teaching device inspired by a fictional columnist who turns what is happening now into a regular practice of noticing and writing.
saints.lesson: Keep a small, reliable update habit. Staying current notices the change; trendsetting decides what to do with it.
saints.whyHere: Carrie Bradshaw is here because staying current is a practice, not a frantic chase after every new release. Her role is to notice what changed and decide whether that change affects your work.
contribution: This is a LAiDIES teaching device inspired by a fictional columnist who turns what is happening now into a regular practice of noticing and writing.
Her lesson is a small, reliable update habit: trendsetting decides what pattern to create; staying current notices the movement that may require a response.
saints.move: Choose a limited set of changes worth tracking—new capability, new risk, changed price, changed policy, or changed expectation. Give each item one question: does this alter a live decision, workflow, or obligation? A currentness habit is useful when it turns noise into a timely decision, not when it fills your day with alerts.
saints.tryIt: Set a short weekly appointment to review one trusted source relevant to a tool you already use. Capture only the change, the source date, and the work question it creates. Check whether the change affects anything you will actually do in the next month. If it does not, archive the note and move on rather than turning attention into a collection habit.
saints.boundary: Staying current does not tell you which trend deserves adoption. That is Cher and Dionne's separate lesson: decide whether a useful pattern is worth making visible and shareable.

concepts.name: Freshness and model drift
concepts.connection: AI products, models, policies and capabilities change, so an earlier answer can become stale without becoming obviously false.

concepts.name: Retrieval and provenance
concepts.connection: Current claims need dated sources that show where the information came from.

concepts.name: Change monitoring
concepts.connection: Useful updating focuses on changes that affect a real decision instead of treating every announcement as urgent.

saints.humanInteraction: A person asks when the information was checked, which source supports it and what changed since the previous decision. She uses AI to compare versions or summarise updates, then verifies the consequential details at the original source.
saints.whyItMattersNow: Teams are making purchasing, policy and workflow decisions in a fast-moving market. A small update habit prevents old model limits, prices, privacy terms or legal assumptions from quietly governing current work.

saints.name: Bette Midler
saints.role: PATRON SAiNT of Doing It All
saints.about: A playful LAiDIES teaching tribute to range: one performer, many modes, each chosen because the work needs it.
saints.lesson: AI is more than text. Use it across images, audio, files, data, code, and whatever combination serves the job.
saints.whyHere: Bette Midler is here because AI is not only a text box. Her role is doing it all: choose across images, audio, files, data, code, and combinations of them according to what the work needs.
contribution: This is a playful LAiDIES teaching tribute to range: one performer, many modes, each chosen because the work needs it.
Her lesson treats AI as a set of different capabilities rather than one generic writing assistant.
saints.move: Start with the actual job, then break it into modes. A proposal might need research notes, a written draft, a chart from data, a visual, and a final human review; those are different pieces of work. Combining modes is valuable only when each one improves the same finished job.
saints.tryIt: Choose one deliverable you already have to make, such as a short client update. List its parts: facts to verify, words to draft, numbers to check, and any image or audio that would genuinely help. Use AI for one or two parts, then assemble the final piece yourself and check that every mode serves the same audience. Remove any AI-made element that is decorative but does not make the decision or message clearer.
saints.boundary: More modes do not automatically make work more complete. A simple text answer can be better than an unnecessary pile of generated assets. This is a LAiDIES teaching tribute, not a biography, endorsement, or claim about Bette Midler’s views on AI.

concepts.name: Multimodal AI
concepts.connection: AI systems can work across text, images, audio, video, code and structured data rather than one medium alone.

concepts.name: Orchestration
concepts.connection: A useful result may require several specialised tools joined into one controlled workflow.

concepts.name: Representation
concepts.connection: The same idea changes when expressed as prose, a chart, an image or a spoken explanation, and each form needs its own review.

saints.humanInteraction: The user decides which medium serves each part of the job, moves material between tools deliberately and checks every transformation. AI may draft the script, analyse the data and create an image, but the person keeps the purpose and the final composition coherent.
saints.whyItMattersNow: Most professional deliverables are already multimodal: a report becomes slides, a meeting becomes actions, or research becomes a campaign. Understanding the whole toolkit lets teams remove repetitive production work without pretending one model is equally good at everything.

saints.name: The Golden Girls
saints.role: PATRON SAiNTS of Never Too Late
saints.about: A LAiDIES teaching ensemble inspired by fictional friends whose experience is an asset, not an expiry date.
saints.lesson: Start at any age or career stage. Bring your judgment with you; technical novelty does not outrank lived experience.
saints.whyHere: The Golden Girls are here because technical novelty does not outrank lived experience. Their role is never too late: start where you are and bring your own judgment with you.
contribution: This is a LAiDIES teaching ensemble inspired by fictional friends whose experience is an asset, not an expiry date.
Their lesson rejects the idea that a new tool requires you to abandon the professional knowledge you already have.
saints.move: Use prior experience as the comparison point for a new tool. You already know what a good client note, safe decision, useful brief, or respectful tone looks like in your field. AI can help you test a new method, but it does not erase the standards you learned by doing the work.
saints.tryIt: Choose one task you know well from experience. Ask AI for a first pass, then compare it with the three signs you personally use to recognise good work in that task. Write down one thing the tool made easier and one thing it still missed. Keep your own criteria in the workflow so the test grows your skill instead of replacing it.
saints.boundary: Experience is valuable, but it is not a reason to ignore a real new risk or capability. The point is to learn without treating novelty as superior by default.

concepts.name: AI literacy
concepts.connection: Understanding inputs, outputs, limitations and checks matters more than performing technical identity.

concepts.name: Domain expertise
concepts.connection: Experience supplies context, exceptions and consequences that a model may not recognise.

concepts.name: Participatory design
concepts.connection: Tools improve when the people affected can shape requirements and evaluate whether the result fits their lives.

saints.humanInteraction: People bring their judgement, relationships and accumulated knowledge into the interaction. They can ask AI to explain unfamiliar terms, challenge its assumptions and compare its suggestion with what actually happens in their work rather than treating technical novelty as seniority.
saints.whyItMattersNow: AI adoption can exclude experienced workers by presenting itself as a generational test. Organisations lose exactly the knowledge needed to spot bad automation when they confuse familiarity with a new interface for understanding the underlying work.

saints.name: Regina George
saints.about: A red-card LAiDIES teaching device inspired by a fictional queen bee who sounds certain enough to make the room stop checking.
saints.lesson: Confidence is not evidence. Slow down when an AI answer is polished, absolute, and conveniently what you wanted to hear.
saints.whyHere: Regina George is the red anti-saint because dangerous confidence can make a room stop checking. Her role is a caution: polished, absolute, convenient answers deserve more scrutiny, not less.
contribution: This is a red-card LAiDIES teaching device inspired by a fictional queen bee who sounds certain enough to make the room stop checking.
Her lesson is that confidence is not evidence, especially when an AI answer says exactly what you wanted to hear.
saints.move: Treat certainty as a signal to inspect the evidence, not as evidence itself. Look for absolute language, missing sources, false precision, and answers that neatly flatter the plan already on the table. A good check asks what would prove this answer wrong before it asks how to make it sound more convincing.
saints.tryIt: Take one AI answer that feels unusually neat or decisive. Underline every absolute claim and every number, then ask for the source, date, and uncertainty behind each one. Check the most important claim against an independent record before sharing it. If the evidence is missing or weak, rewrite the answer as a question or leave it out.
saints.boundary: Uncertainty is not the same as paralysis, and confidence is not always wrong. The anti-saint exists to stop confidence from doing the checking in place of you.

concepts.name: Calibration
concepts.connection: Confidence should match the strength of the evidence; fluent language is not a probability estimate.

concepts.name: Hallucination
concepts.connection: Generative systems can produce plausible statements, citations and explanations that are unsupported or invented.

concepts.name: Confirmation and automation bias
concepts.connection: People are especially likely to accept a polished answer when it agrees with what they wanted to believe.

saints.humanInteraction: The user creates friction at the moment an answer feels irresistibly convenient. She asks for sources, searches for disconfirming evidence and separates the model's wording from the decision she is accountable for. A second confident response from the same system is not independent confirmation.
saints.whyItMattersNow: AI can make weak claims sound executive-ready in seconds. The greatest risk is often not an obviously absurd answer, but a tidy conclusion that moves through a meeting because nobody wants to interrupt its confidence.

mavens.name: Ada Lovelace
mavens.about: Her 1843 Notes on the Analytical Engine include a worked method for calculating Bernoulli numbers.
mavens.lesson: A useful program is a precise sequence, not a magic answer.
mavens.freshness: Historical contribution and destinations checked 2 Sep 2026
mavens.whyHere: Ada Lovelace is here because her 1843 Notes make a program visible as a worked method, not a mysterious machine trick. Her Bernoulli-number method gives this room a concrete starting point for talking about instructions.
contribution: In her 1843 Notes on the Analytical Engine, Lovelace included a worked method for calculating Bernoulli numbers.
That surviving example matters because it shows an intended result being reached through an ordered method rather than through an answer appearing by itself.
mavens.move: In LAiDIES terms, borrow the move of making the steps inspectable. When an AI result matters, the useful thing is not only the final paragraph, table, or image; it is the sequence of choices, inputs, and checks that produced it. A sequence can be revised and shared, unlike a magic answer.
mavens.tryIt: Choose one repeated task, such as turning meeting notes into a project update. Write the steps you currently take before asking AI to help with any one of them. Ask it for a first pass, then have the workflow owner compare that pass with the stated purpose and original notes. Keep the workflow only if another person could follow the steps and reproduce a result the owner would stand behind.
mavens.boundary: This is a LAiDIES teaching interpretation of Lovelace's worked method, not a claim that she taught present-day AI practice. A documented sequence still needs human judgment about whether the result is correct and appropriate.

concepts.name: Algorithms
concepts.connection: An algorithm is an ordered method for transforming defined inputs into a result.

concepts.name: Task decomposition
concepts.connection: A complex objective becomes executable when it is broken into operations and intermediate values.

concepts.name: Reproducibility
concepts.connection: Documented steps allow another person to inspect, repeat and revise the method.

mavens.humanInteraction: People define the objective, inputs, sequence and checks before a machine can execute the procedure. With generative AI, those instructions may be conversational rather than coded, but the human still determines what counts as the right task and an acceptable result.
mavens.whyItMattersNow: Repeatable AI work depends on more than saving a clever prompt. Teams need the source material, sequence, decision points and human checks that turn one successful output into a process another person can safely reproduce.

mavens.name: Grace Hopper
mavens.about: She worked on the Mark I, developed early compiler work, and later helped develop and promote COBOL.
mavens.lesson: Clearer instructions make powerful systems more usable.

links.label: Watch Grace Hopper discuss the Mark I

mavens.freshness: Historical contribution and destinations checked 2 Sep 2026
mavens.whyHere: Grace Hopper is here because her work makes a central computing problem plain: people need ways to express an intention that a machine can carry out. Her Mark I, compiler, and COBOL work connects that problem across different stages of computing.
contribution: Hopper worked on the Mark I, developed early compiler work, and later helped develop and promote COBOL.
Together, those documented contributions show that making instructions clearer and more usable is part of making computing useful.
mavens.move: In LAiDIES terms, state the job before you ask for the output. A good instruction tells a tool what it is trying to produce, what material it may use, and what a usable answer has to include. That is clearer than treating a prompt as a wish made to a black box.
mavens.tryIt: Take one instruction your team gives repeatedly, such as turning meeting notes into a client follow-up. Ask the person who receives the result to circle every verb or term that could be interpreted two ways, then replace each ambiguity with a concrete operation or example. Save the repaired instruction as a reusable translation layer between the team’s intent and the tool. Keep it only if a second person can use it correctly without an oral explanation.
mavens.boundary: This profile does not claim that a clear instruction guarantees a correct result. A machine can follow a well-formed request and still use weak source material or make a bad inference.

concepts.name: Compilers
concepts.connection: A compiler translates human-written instructions into forms a computer can execute.

concepts.name: Abstraction
concepts.connection: Higher-level languages let people express intent without controlling every machine-level detail.

concepts.name: Interface design
concepts.connection: The language between person and machine determines who can use computing power and how precisely.

mavens.humanInteraction: AI interfaces mediate between a user's instructions and system operations, but that mediation is not a faithful compiler-style translation. People choose words, examples or controls to express the job, then still need to check how the system interpreted them.
mavens.whyItMattersNow: Natural-language AI feels effortless because much of the technical translation is hidden. Understanding that translation still occurs helps workers specify intent, recognise misinterpretation and avoid treating conversational ease as proof that the system understood the business context.

mavens.name: Hedy Lamarr
mavens.about: Lamarr and George Antheil patented a frequency-hopping communication system in 1942; that is narrower and more accurate than saying she invented Wi-Fi.
mavens.lesson: An idea can take a long, indirect route into later technology.

links.label: Read the Inventors Hall of Fame profile

mavens.freshness: Historical contribution and destinations checked 2 Sep 2026
mavens.whyHere: Hedy Lamarr is here because the record is more interesting than the shortcut: she and George Antheil patented a frequency-hopping communication system in 1942. It is a useful reminder to trace a real technical contribution precisely rather than flattening it into a flattering myth.
contribution: Lamarr and Antheil patented a frequency-hopping communication system in 1942.
Lamarr did not invent Wi-Fi. Her frequency-hopping patent became one part of a much longer, indirect technological lineage.
mavens.move: In LAiDIES terms, design for a communication path to keep working when one route becomes noisy, unavailable, or unreliable. Do not confuse robustness with magical resilience: name the likely interruption, the alternate route, and the point where a person must take over.
mavens.tryIt: Choose one AI-assisted handoff your team depends on, such as routing a customer request or sending approved notes into a drafting tool. Name one realistic interruption: the integration fails, the model is unavailable, or the input arrives in the wrong format. Test the alternate route with a harmless example and record who notices the failure, how the work continues, and when the normal route is restored. If the backup exists only in someone's memory, the workflow is not robust yet.
mavens.boundary: This is not a lesson that every later technology has one neat inventor. Technical change is often collaborative, layered, and indirect.

concepts.name: Frequency hopping
concepts.connection: Changing channels according to a shared pattern can make a radio signal harder to jam.

concepts.name: Robust communication
concepts.connection: A system can be designed to keep functioning when its communication environment is contested or unreliable.

concepts.name: Technology lineage
concepts.connection: Later systems may inherit an idea indirectly; resemblance is not proof of a simple one-inventor story.

mavens.humanInteraction: People experience AI through networks, devices and services that must communicate reliably. They choose whether a system can operate offline, what happens when a connection fails and whether a later product genuinely traces to the innovation being cited.
mavens.whyItMattersNow: AI products are built on layers of communications infrastructure and long chains of prior research. Accurate lineage prevents inspirational storytelling from replacing evidence and reminds teams to design for interruption, interference and failure.

mavens.name: Karen Spärck Jones
mavens.about: A pioneer in information retrieval and natural-language processing, she introduced inverse-document-frequency term weighting.
mavens.lesson: Search improves when a system weighs what distinguishes a term, not merely whether it appears.

links.label: Read Cambridge’s Karen Spärck Jones archive
Watch Karen Spärck Jones’s award lecture

mavens.freshness: Historical contribution and destinations checked 2 Sep 2026
mavens.whyHere: Karen Spärck Jones is here because search becomes more useful when a system notices what makes a term distinctive, not merely frequent. Her inverse-document-frequency work gives a reader a way to see why some results rise above a pile of similar-looking material.
contribution: Spärck Jones was a pioneer in information retrieval and natural-language processing, and she introduced inverse-document-frequency term weighting.
That work gives search systems a way to weigh terms by how much they help distinguish one document from another.
mavens.move: In LAiDIES terms, search with the detail that separates your real question from the crowd. A request for 'AI policy' invites a broad pile; a request naming the decision, audience, sector, or constraint gives a retrieval system more to distinguish. The point is not fancy wording but making the useful difference visible.
mavens.tryIt: Take one research search that returned too much. Add two details that would genuinely separate your case, such as a jurisdiction and the decision you are making. Ask the research owner to compare the first five results from both searches for relevance to the actual question. Keep the narrower wording only if it improves the evidence that person can use, not just the number of results.
mavens.boundary: More distinctive terms do not make a source trustworthy. Search ranking can help you find material; it cannot decide whether that material is current, accurate, or right for your situation.

concepts.name: Information retrieval
concepts.connection: Retrieval finds and ranks material that may answer a question rather than generating the answer itself.

concepts.name: Inverse document frequency
concepts.connection: A term can be more informative when it is rare across the wider collection than when it appears everywhere.

concepts.name: Retrieval-augmented generation
concepts.connection: Modern AI systems can retrieve documents before generating, but the quality of the source set and ranking still governs what reaches the model.

mavens.humanInteraction: The user shapes retrieval through the query, the collection being searched and the judgement applied to the ranked results. When an AI answer cites retrieved material, the person still checks whether the chosen passage is relevant and supports the claim.
mavens.whyItMattersNow: Search and retrieval sit underneath workplace copilots, knowledge assistants and many apparent question-answering systems. The retrieval stage cannot supply evidence it did not find or that the organisation never indexed. A generator may still produce an answer from model parameters, but that answer lacks the missing retrieved support.

mavens.name: Hannah Fry
mavens.about: Cambridge lists Fry as Professor of the Public Understanding of Mathematics.
mavens.lesson: Make an invisible technical system understandable by showing where it touches ordinary decisions.

links.label: Listen to The Rest Is Science
Listen to Google DeepMind: The Podcast

mavens.whyHere: Hannah Fry is here because the LUMINAiRY needs someone who makes a technical idea legible where it touches an ordinary decision. Cambridge lists Fry as Professor of the Public Understanding of Mathematics, which gives this profile its clear teaching job.
contribution: Cambridge lists Hannah Fry as Professor of the Public Understanding of Mathematics.

Her public-understanding work is useful here because it begins where a technical system meets an ordinary decision. The explanation has to reveal what the system receives, what it changes, where it can fail, and what the reader still has to decide.
mavens.move: In LAiDIES terms, do not begin an explanation with the tool's name or a stack of jargon. Begin with the decision a person has to make, then show what information goes in, what the system changes, and what could go wrong. That gives a reader something to inspect rather than merely something to admire.
mavens.tryIt: Choose one AI feature your team is considering, such as a meeting-summary tool. Explain it to a colleague in four sentences: what it receives, what it produces, where a person still has to check it, and what a bad result could affect. Ask the colleague to tell you the process back. Revise until they can describe the decision point without borrowing your jargon.
mavens.boundary: This is a LAiDIES interpretation built from Fry's documented public-understanding role, not a claim that she endorses this particular workplace exercise. A clear explanation does not settle whether a system should be used.

concepts.name: AI literacy
concepts.connection: People need a usable mental model of what a system receives, changes and returns before they can judge it.

concepts.name: Explainability
concepts.connection: An explanation makes the relevant mechanism and decision points visible without pretending every internal detail is knowable.

concepts.name: Socio-technical systems
concepts.connection: An algorithm matters where it meets people, institutions, incentives and consequences.

mavens.humanInteraction: A person begins with the human decision, then asks what data enters the system, what the system changes, where error can appear and who retains authority. She tests understanding by explaining the process back in ordinary language rather than repeating product vocabulary.
mavens.whyItMattersNow: AI is used across hiring, healthcare, education, media and office work, often through systems whose technical internals users cannot inspect. Clear mental models let non-specialists ask better questions without giving them false confidence that a simple explanation settles every risk.

mavens.name: Fei-Fei Li
mavens.about: Li is Stanford’s Sequoia Professor and a founding co-director of Stanford HAI; Stanford identifies her as an inventor of ImageNet, and World Labs identifies her as co-founder and CEO.
mavens.lesson: Training data turns human labels into a model’s idea of the world—ask who chose the examples and what they leave out.

links.label: Read Fei-Fei Li on spatial intelligence
Watch Fei-Fei Li discuss world models

mavens.whyHere: Fei-Fei Li is here because training data is not background scenery: it teaches a system which examples and categories count. Her documented work on ImageNet makes that hidden layer of AI easier to see.
contribution: Stanford identifies Li as an inventor of ImageNet; it also lists her as Sequoia Professor and a founding co-director of Stanford HAI.
World Labs identifies her as its co-founder and CEO, linking her current work to a continuing public conversation about how AI represents the world.
mavens.move: In LAiDIES terms, ask where a model's categories came from before you treat them as natural facts. Examples were selected, labelled, and grouped by people; that process shapes what a system can recognise and what it may miss. The practical question is not only 'does it work?' but also 'what did it learn from?'.
mavens.tryIt: Before using an AI-generated classification, shortlist, or image description in a work decision, write down the examples or labels it seems to be relying on. Check one edge case that matters to the people affected by your decision. If you cannot identify an appropriate source or test case, do not turn the output into a final judgment. Save the question you could not answer for the person responsible for the tool.
mavens.boundary: A training-set question can reveal a risk; it cannot on its own prove that a particular model is fair or unfit for every use. The relevant test depends on the decision and who carries its consequences.

concepts.name: Training data
concepts.connection: Models learn statistical patterns from data whose collection and organisation reflect human choices; supervised datasets also depend on human-defined labels.

concepts.name: Computer vision
concepts.connection: Vision systems turn pixels into predictions about objects, scenes and relationships.

concepts.name: Representation and bias
concepts.connection: What the dataset includes, excludes and labels shapes what the model can recognise and how errors are distributed.

mavens.humanInteraction: People interact with the model long before they type a prompt: they collect examples, define categories and decide which labels count as truth. Later users encounter those decisions when the system recognises some situations reliably and misreads others.
mavens.whyItMattersNow: Training data now influences image search, medical imaging, robotics and generative systems. Teams buying or building AI need to ask whose world the examples represent and whether evaluation covers the people and conditions in the real deployment.

mavens.name: Timnit Gebru
mavens.about: DAIR identifies Gebru as its founder and executive director. She co-authored the peer-reviewed paper On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots.
mavens.lesson: A fluent answer can still be unreliable: ask what data, labour, and incentives produced it before treating it as knowledge.

links.label: Read On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots

mavens.whyHere: Timnit Gebru is here because a fluent system can look knowledgeable before anyone has asked what made it possible. Her work gives the room a disciplined way to question the data, labour, and incentives behind an AI claim.
contribution: DAIR identifies Gebru as its founder and executive director.
Her co-authored paper On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots examines how apparently fluent language-model output can obscure the data, labour, scale, and institutional incentives that produced it.
mavens.move: In LAiDIES terms, treat fluency as something to investigate, not a credential. Ask what source material, human work, and organisational incentives sit behind a confident answer before relying on it as knowledge. That question changes the job from admiring an output to examining its conditions.
mavens.tryIt: Take one polished AI answer you are tempted to reuse. Alongside its factual claims, make three columns: whose data may have shaped it, whose labour made or checked that data, and whose incentives influence how the system is presented. Ask the decision-maker to mark what is known, assumed, or missing and who could be harmed by the gap. If a consequential unknown remains, use the output to frame questions rather than as evidence.
mavens.boundary: This is not a claim that every fluent answer is false. It is a reminder that confidence, polish, and truth are different things.

concepts.name: Large language models
concepts.connection: Scale can increase capability while also increasing the cost, opacity and reach of failures.

concepts.name: Dataset documentation
concepts.connection: The origin, composition, labour and intended use of training data affect what claims can responsibly be made about a model.

concepts.name: Power and accountability
concepts.connection: Technical choices are shaped by institutions and incentives, and their harms are not distributed evenly.

mavens.humanInteraction: A user asks what produced the fluent answer: which data, whose labour, what optimisation target and what business incentive. She treats the output as the result of a system with a history and owner, not disembodied knowledge arriving from nowhere.
mavens.whyItMattersNow: Organisations can adopt powerful models without visibility into their training or failure patterns. Documentation, external scrutiny and the ability to challenge deployment are practical safeguards when scale makes individual errors easier to spread.

mavens.name: Rachel Thomas
mavens.about: Thomas is a co-founder of fast.ai. Her site describes her as the founding director of the Center for Applied Data Ethics and a Professor of Practice at Queensland University of Technology’s Centre for Data Science.
mavens.lesson: Good AI teaching should include the task, its likely harms, and the people affected—not only the fastest way to use the tool.

links.label: Read fast.ai’s Applied Data Ethics course
Watch Rachel Thomas teach data ethics

mavens.whyHere: Rachel Thomas is here because learning to use AI is incomplete if the lesson leaves out who may be affected by the task. Her fast.ai and applied-data-ethics work makes room for the human stakes alongside technical capability.
contribution: Thomas is a co-founder of fast.ai and the founding director of the Center for Applied Data Ethics.
Her own site also describes her as a Professor of Practice at Queensland University of Technology's Centre for Data Science.
mavens.move: In LAiDIES terms, put the task, likely harm, and affected people in the same brief. A tool can make a workflow faster while shifting the burden of its mistakes onto someone who had no say in it. Naming that possibility early creates a better question than 'can we automate this?'.
mavens.tryIt: Choose one AI-assisted workflow your team already uses or wants to try. Write three lines before the next test: the decision it supports, who could be harmed by a wrong result, and who will review the output. Run a small example and ask the reviewer whether the likely harm was visible in the workflow. Do not call the test successful only because it was fast.
mavens.boundary: This practice cannot predict every consequence or replace affected people's expertise. It is a way to make a missing question present before a workflow hardens around it.

concepts.name: Applied data ethics
concepts.connection: Ethical analysis begins with the concrete system, affected people and plausible pathways to harm.

concepts.name: Participatory design
concepts.connection: People who bear the consequences should influence requirements, testing and deployment decisions.

concepts.name: AI education
concepts.connection: Teaching technical use without consequences creates capability without judgement.

mavens.humanInteraction: The practitioner maps who provides the data, who receives the output, who can contest it and who is missing from the design room. She uses AI skills together with questions about power and consequence rather than treating ethics as a final approval box.
mavens.whyItMattersNow: Workplace AI pilots can move from demonstration to policy before affected employees or customers are consulted. Bringing ethics into task selection and testing prevents teams from efficiently automating a decision they should have redesigned first.

mavens.name: Joy Buolamwini
mavens.about: Buolamwini is founder of the Algorithmic Justice League and author of Unmasking AI. Her Gender Shades work evaluated commercial gender-classification systems across skin type and gender.
mavens.lesson: Test error rates across the people who will bear the consequences, not only the overall average.

links.label: Watch Joy Buolamwini discuss Unmasking AI

mavens.whyHere: Joy Buolamwini is here because an average score can hide who carries the error. Her Gender Shades work makes the question concrete by evaluating commercial gender-classification systems across skin type and gender.
contribution: Buolamwini founded the Algorithmic Justice League and wrote *Unmasking AI*.
Her Gender Shades work evaluated commercial gender-classification systems across skin type and gender rather than treating one overall figure as the whole story.
mavens.move: In LAiDIES terms, do not accept a single success rate when different people may receive different outcomes. Break the test into the groups who would actually bear the consequences and look for uneven error. The move is not to make a prettier metric; it is to discover whether the metric is hiding a human problem.
mavens.tryIt: If you use an AI-assisted screening, recommendation, or classification process, choose the groups for whom a wrong result would matter most. Test a small set of representative cases and record where the output fails or becomes uncertain. Ask a person with responsibility for the decision to review those failures before the process is expanded. A strong overall average is not a substitute for that review.
mavens.boundary: Small local tests do not establish that a system is fair across every group or context. They are a prompt to investigate uneven consequences, not a fairness certificate.

concepts.name: Algorithmic bias
concepts.connection: A system can perform differently across demographic groups because of data, design and evaluation choices.

concepts.name: Disaggregated evaluation
concepts.connection: Overall accuracy can hide severe error rates for smaller or marginalised groups.

concepts.name: Facial analysis
concepts.connection: Systems that classify or identify faces can create unequal errors and high-stakes consequences.

mavens.humanInteraction: People decide which groups appear in the test, which error matters and whether anyone can challenge a result. A user or buyer can demand subgroup evidence instead of accepting one impressive average as proof that the system works for everyone.
mavens.whyItMattersNow: AI evaluation increasingly influences purchasing and deployment. Disaggregated testing makes hidden failure visible before a tool reaches hiring, identity verification, public services or other settings where the people misread by the system bear the cost.

mavens.name: Kate Crawford
mavens.about: Crawford is a research professor at USC, a senior principal researcher at Microsoft Research New York, and the inaugural visiting chair of AI and Justice at the École Normale Supérieure in Paris.
mavens.lesson: AI has a supply chain—minerals, labour, energy, data, and institutional power—so assess it beyond the screen.

links.label: Read Atlas of AI from Yale

mavens.whyHere: Kate Crawford is here because an AI product does not begin and end at the screen. Her work gives the LUMINAiRY a way to see the materials, labour, energy, data, and institutional power around a system.
contribution: Crawford is a research professor at USC, a senior principal researcher at Microsoft Research New York, and the inaugural visiting chair of AI and Justice at the École Normale Supérieure in Paris.

Her work traces AI beyond the visible interface to a supply chain of minerals, labour, energy, data, and institutional power. That wider boundary changes what must be considered before a system is called simple or harmless.
mavens.move: In LAiDIES terms, draw the system boundary wider before deciding that a tool is simple or harmless. Ask what it needs: data, energy, people doing hidden work, and an institution making choices about power and access. The point is not to make every decision impossible, but to stop calling the unseen parts irrelevant.
mavens.tryIt: Before recommending an AI tool, make a one-page map with five headings: data, people, energy, access, and decision-maker. Put one verified fact or unanswered question under each heading. Check the map with the person responsible for procurement, privacy, or the workflow before you call the tool ready. Keep unanswered questions visible instead of converting them into assumptions.
mavens.boundary: A map is not a complete impact assessment and does not tell you the right answer by itself. It makes the conditions of the decision visible enough for someone to take responsibility for them.

concepts.name: AI supply chains
concepts.connection: Models depend on minerals, energy, data centres, human labour, datasets and institutional infrastructure.

concepts.name: Externalities
concepts.connection: Some costs of an AI product fall on people and places outside the buyer's immediate view.

concepts.name: Political economy
concepts.connection: Who owns infrastructure, data and decision power shapes which systems are built and whose interests they serve.

mavens.humanInteraction: A person looks beyond the interface and asks what resources, labour and permissions make the feature possible. Procurement and product decisions become part of AI interaction because choosing a system also chooses its supply chain and governance.
mavens.whyItMattersNow: Generative AI is often evaluated through output quality alone. Organisations making climate, labour, privacy or public-interest commitments need to examine the material and institutional costs that remain invisible in a convenient chat window.

mavens.name: Meredith Whittaker
mavens.about: Whittaker is President of Signal, Chief Advisor and former Faculty Director of the AI Now Institute, which she co-founded.
mavens.lesson: Privacy is infrastructure: change what a system is allowed to collect, and you change what it can know and do.

links.label: Read Meredith Whittaker at AI Now
Read Meredith Whittaker on Signal’s mission
Read Meredith Whittaker on open-source AI
Listen to Meredith Whittaker on algorithmic oversight

mavens.whyHere: Meredith Whittaker is here because privacy is a design condition, not a reassuring sentence at the end of a product page. Her work across Signal and the AI Now Institute makes the relationship between data collection and power visible.
contribution: Whittaker is President of Signal and Chief Advisor and former Faculty Director of the AI Now Institute, which she co-founded.
Her public work spans Signal's mission, AI Now, and open-source AI.
mavens.move: In LAiDIES terms, ask what a system is permitted to collect before you ask what it can do. Collecting less limits direct exposure and can reduce the opportunities for sensitive inferences, although proxy data may still reveal things a person never supplied explicitly. That makes privacy a practical part of system design.
mavens.tryIt: For one AI feature you use, list every category of information it receives before producing an answer. Mark which categories are necessary for the task and which are merely convenient. Ask the workflow owner to explain why each nonessential category is present. Do not paste sensitive material into the system while that question remains unanswered.
mavens.boundary: Collecting less data does not make a system safe in every other respect. Privacy is one design condition alongside security, accuracy, access, and accountable use.

concepts.name: Data minimisation
concepts.connection: Collecting and retaining less information reduces direct exposure and opportunities for later use, although proxy data can still enable sensitive inferences.

concepts.name: Surveillance business models
concepts.connection: Revenue and institutional incentives can encourage systems to gather more behavioural data than the immediate service requires.

concepts.name: Privacy infrastructure
concepts.connection: Architecture, defaults and governance protect privacy more reliably than promises placed around unrestricted collection.

mavens.humanInteraction: People shape what an AI system can know by choosing which provider, permissions and data path they use. They can remove unnecessary inputs, prefer privacy-preserving services and challenge features that require broad collection for a narrow benefit.
mavens.whyItMattersNow: AI features are being added to communications and workplace platforms that already hold sensitive information. Privacy decisions made in infrastructure determine future possibilities for profiling, training and surveillance long after the original convenience has been forgotten.

mavens.name: Emily M. Bender
mavens.about: Bender is the Thomas L. and Margo G. Wyckoff Endowed Professor in the University of Washington Department of Linguistics, Faculty Director of the Professional MS in Computational Linguistics, and Director of the Computational Linguistics Laboratory.
mavens.lesson: Plausible wording is not understanding: ask what evidence connects a model’s output to the world before relying on it.

links.label: Follow Emily M. Bender on Mastodon
Follow Emily M. Bender on X

mavens.whyHere: Emily Bender is here because a sentence can sound convincing without being connected to the world it describes. Her work in linguistics gives the room language for separating plausible wording from warranted reliance.
contribution: Bender is the Thomas L. and Margo G. Wyckoff Endowed Professor in the University of Washington Department of Linguistics, Faculty Director of the Professional MS in Computational Linguistics, and Director of the Computational Linguistics Laboratory.
Her work draws a necessary line between plausible wording and grounded, warranted claims. A language model can produce the former without establishing the latter.
mavens.move: In LAiDIES terms, ask what evidence connects an AI answer to the actual situation before acting on it. A fluent paragraph may be useful as a draft, a summary to check, or a prompt for research; it is not automatically a report of what is true. The important distinction is between a string of likely words and a claim with support.
mavens.tryIt: Take one AI-written paragraph you want to send externally. Mark each sentence as observed fact, inference, or wording suggestion. For every fact, replace the model's phrasing with the exact supported detail from an approved record; for every inference, name the human owner willing to stand behind it. Remove any first-person or authoritative flourish that makes generated language sound like witnessed knowledge.
mavens.boundary: Source checking does not mean that language models have no useful role. It means the role changes with the consequence of being wrong.

concepts.name: Language modelling
concepts.connection: A language model predicts likely continuations from patterns in its training data.

concepts.name: Meaning and grounding
concepts.connection: Plausible language does not by itself establish a connection to the world, evidence or a speaker's intent.

concepts.name: Anthropomorphism
concepts.connection: Human-sounding responses can lead users to attribute understanding, beliefs or authority the system has not demonstrated.

mavens.humanInteraction: The user separates conversational fluency from knowledge. She asks what source or observation grounds the answer, avoids treating first-person language as evidence of a mind and uses the model for language work without assigning it human accountability.
mavens.whyItMattersNow: Chat interfaces make statistical text generation feel like a social exchange. Keeping the mechanism visible helps workers use fluency productively while checking facts, protecting sensitive information and reserving consequential judgement for people.

mavens.name: The ENIAC Six
mavens.about: The six original ENIAC programmers—Kathleen McNulty Mauchly Antonelli, Jean Jennings Bartik, Frances Elizabeth Holberton, Marlyn Wescoff Meltzer, Frances Bilas Spence, and Ruth Lichterman Teitelbaum—developed programming techniques including subroutines and nesting.
mavens.lesson: Programming was technical work from the beginning, even when the people doing it were written out of the story.

links.label: Read about the Women of ENIAC
Watch the ENIAC Programmers Project documentary
Read the Smithsonian ENIAC videohistory archive

mavens.freshness: Historical contribution and destinations checked 2 Sep 2026
mavens.whyHere: The ENIAC Six are here because programming was technical work from the beginning, even when the people doing it were written out of the story. Their documented techniques make it impossible to treat early programming as an afterthought.
contribution: The six original ENIAC programmers were Kathleen McNulty Mauchly Antonelli, Jean Jennings Bartik, Frances Elizabeth Holberton, Marlyn Wescoff Meltzer, Frances Bilas Spence, and Ruth Lichterman Teitelbaum.
They developed programming techniques including subroutines and nesting.
mavens.move: In LAiDIES terms, look for the work hidden behind a finished system. When a tool appears to produce an answer effortlessly, ask who designed the steps, defined the pieces that can be reused, and made the process dependable. That question gives credit more accurately and reveals where the real expertise lives.
mavens.tryIt: Choose one AI-assisted process in your team that now feels automatic. List the people who supplied source material, shaped the instruction, checked the output, and decided when it could be used. Check the list with the team before describing the result as the tool's work alone. Use what you find to clarify ownership of the next revision.
mavens.boundary: This group profile honours a shared contribution; it does not pretend one short card can recover each woman's full story or treat the six women as interchangeable.

concepts.name: Programming
concepts.connection: Programming turns a mathematical or operational objective into a sequence a machine can execute.

concepts.name: Human infrastructure
concepts.connection: Technical systems rely on skilled labour that documentation and public stories may erase.

concepts.name: Procedural knowledge
concepts.connection: Operating a new machine often requires people to invent methods before formal tools or job categories exist.

mavens.humanInteraction: People are part of the computing system: they translate problems, configure processes, detect failures and create the operating knowledge around new technology. In many AI systems, less-visible review, labelling and workflow labour materially affects whether the visible model works in practice.
mavens.whyItMattersNow: Organisations often describe AI as replacing work while quietly relying on people to prepare data, correct outputs and handle exceptions. Naming that labour improves planning, credit, staffing and accountability instead of hiding essential work behind automation language.

mavens.name: Margaret Hamilton
mavens.about: Hamilton led MIT’s Software Engineering Division for Apollo guidance work. NASA and MIT describe her as leading the team that developed Apollo flight software; this card retains that team boundary.
mavens.lesson: When a system faces too many demands at once, its priority rules can determine whether it fails safely or fails badly.

links.label: Read Margaret Hamilton’s Apollo software record
Read the Smithsonian Apollo flight-software archive
Watch MIT’s Margaret Hamilton video spotlight

mavens.freshness: Historical contribution and destinations checked 2 Sep 2026
mavens.whyHere: Margaret Hamilton is here because software has to decide what happens when a system is asked to do too much at once. Her Apollo work makes priority rules and safe failure visible as design choices.
contribution: Hamilton led MIT's Software Engineering Division for Apollo guidance work.
NASA and MIT describe her as leading the team that developed Apollo flight software; this profile keeps that team boundary rather than turning the work into a lone-hero story.
mavens.move: In LAiDIES terms, decide in advance what your workflow must protect when inputs conflict, arrive late, or exceed capacity. A system's priorities determine which task waits, which task stops, and when a person must take over. That is more useful than assuming that a polished interface means the process knows what matters most.
mavens.tryIt: Pick an AI-assisted workflow that handles more than one request, such as triaging customer messages. Write the two things it must never sacrifice, such as a safety escalation or a contractual deadline. Test a deliberately conflicting example and check whether the workflow surfaces the conflict to a human. If it cannot, do not automate the final decision.
mavens.boundary: A small office workflow is not Apollo guidance software, and the analogy stops there. The transferable point is only that priority rules and handoff conditions should be designed, not assumed.

concepts.name: Software engineering
concepts.connection: Reliable software requires designed processes, interfaces, tests and failure handling—not code alone.

concepts.name: Priority scheduling
concepts.connection: When a system cannot process everything, rules determine which work continues and which is deferred.

concepts.name: Fault tolerance
concepts.connection: A system is designed to recognise overload or error and preserve the most critical function.

mavens.humanInteraction: People define which outcomes are mission-critical, test overload conditions and decide what the system should do when information conflicts. With AI, fallback behaviour and escalation paths are as important as the ideal demonstration.
mavens.whyItMattersNow: AI is moving into workflows where failures interrupt customers, employees and public services. Teams need to design for bad inputs, unavailable models and competing demands before a polished pilot is allowed to become infrastructure.

mavens.name: Frances Allen
mavens.about: Allen was an IBM computer scientist whose work on optimizing compiler techniques and automatic parallel execution laid foundations for modern optimizing compilers. She was the first woman to receive the ACM A.M. Turing Award.
mavens.lesson: A compiler does not merely translate instructions: it reorganises them so a machine can do the same job more efficiently.

links.label: Read Frances Allen’s ACM Turing Award citation
Watch Frances Allen’s ACM oral-history video

mavens.freshness: Historical contribution and destinations checked 2 Sep 2026
mavens.whyHere: Frances Allen is here because getting the same job done more efficiently is not the same as changing the job's purpose. Her compiler and parallel-execution work makes optimisation a visible design choice rather than a magic speed-up.
contribution: Allen was an IBM computer scientist whose work on optimizing compiler techniques and automatic parallel execution laid foundations for modern optimizing compilers.
She was the first woman to receive the ACM A.M. Turing Award.
mavens.move: In LAiDIES terms, improve a workflow without losing the condition that made it useful. A compiler can reorganise instructions so that a machine performs the same job more efficiently; similarly, an AI workflow should be measured against the outcome it is meant to preserve. Faster output that loses the essential check is not an optimisation.
mavens.tryIt: Choose one slow, repeatable drafting task. Measure the time you spend now and name one quality condition the finished work must retain, such as every claim being sourced. Test an AI-assisted version, then have the workflow owner check both time and the named condition. Keep it only if it improves the first without weakening the second.
mavens.boundary: Efficiency is not the only value in a work system. Some tasks need deliberation, privacy protection, or human review even when automation could make them faster.

concepts.name: Compiler optimisation
concepts.connection: A compiler can reorganise instructions to execute the same intended computation more efficiently.

concepts.name: Parallel computing
concepts.connection: Work can be divided so multiple operations proceed at the same time when dependencies allow it.

concepts.name: Efficiency
concepts.connection: Performance gains depend on understanding the structure of the computation, not merely using faster hardware.

mavens.humanInteraction: Users rarely see optimisation directly, but they choose workloads, latency expectations and quality settings that determine how much computation is spent. Engineers decide which transformations preserve the intended result and which trade speed against cost or precision.
mavens.whyItMattersNow: Training and running AI models can consume substantial compute. Better software and parallel execution affect cost, response time and energy use, making efficiency a product and governance decision rather than a purely technical afterthought.

mavens.name: Grace Wahba
mavens.about: Grace Wahba is Professor Emerita at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. UW identifies her smoothing-spline work as foundational to modern data science and machine learning.
mavens.lesson: A good model follows the signal while penalising needless wiggle: test whether extra detail improves the decision, not merely the fit.

links.label: Read Grace Wahba’s research and publications
Read how smoothing splines shaped data science
