mavens.whyHere: Grace Wahba belongs here because her smoothing-spline work helped establish a practical question at the heart of data science: how do you follow a real pattern without chasing every wobble? UW–Madison describes that work as foundational to modern data science and machine learning.
contribution: A model can be made more detailed and still become less useful. Wahba’s work makes that trade-off visible: it rewards a curve for following the signal, while penalising needless wiggle.
That matters whenever an AI system appears impressively tailored to old examples. A close fit is not automatically a good decision rule if the extra detail is merely memorising noise.
mavens.move: LAiDIES interpretation: ask whether an extra layer of detail changes the decision you need to make, rather than whether it makes a result look more precise. This is not a rule to make every model simple; it is a prompt to make complexity earn its place.
mavens.tryIt: Take one recurring forecast or AI-generated classification and set aside a small batch of new cases that were not used to tune the workflow. Compare the current system with a simpler baseline on those held-out cases, using the error that matters to the decision. Keep the extra complexity only if it improves performance beyond the examples the system already saw; otherwise mark it as overfitting risk rather than sophistication.
mavens.boundary: This profile draws one lesson from smoothing-spline work; it does not claim that Wahba personally endorsed this workplace practice. A good-looking fit cannot replace testing on the real decision and context.

concepts.name: Regularisation
concepts.connection: A model is penalised for needless complexity so it follows durable signal rather than every fluctuation.

concepts.name: Overfitting
concepts.connection: A system can match its training examples closely while performing poorly on new cases.

concepts.name: Generalisation
concepts.connection: The real test is whether a learned pattern remains useful beyond the data used to fit it.

mavens.humanInteraction: People choose how much complexity to allow and test the model on examples it did not learn from. A user encountering a beautifully tailored prediction should ask whether the apparent precision survives a new customer, month or operating condition.
mavens.whyItMattersNow: AI systems are often selected using impressive historical performance. Regularisation and out-of-sample testing explain why a simpler model may be more trustworthy for future work than one that perfectly memorised yesterday.

mavens.name: Cynthia Dwork
mavens.about: Cynthia Dwork is Gordon McKay Professor of Computer Science at Harvard SEAS, affiliated faculty at Harvard Law School and the Department of Statistics, and founder of the Hire Aspirations Institute.
mavens.lesson: Ask what can be learned about a group while making each person’s participation hard to infer: privacy is a measurable property, not a promise.

links.label: Watch Cynthia Dwork’s Harvard Ding Shum Lecture

mavens.whyHere: Cynthia Dwork belongs here because she co-invented differential privacy, helping put privacy-preserving data analysis on a mathematically rigorous foundation. Her work makes protection a property to examine, not merely a reassuring sentence in a policy.
contribution: Dwork and her collaborators developed the foundational theory of differential privacy: a strong guarantee designed to limit how much an analysis reveals about whether one particular person's data was included.
For AI work, the distinction matters because a useful dashboard, model, or summary can still expose too much about an individual if its inputs, outputs, or access rules are poorly designed.
mavens.move: LAiDIES interpretation: before sharing an AI-assisted analysis, distinguish what the group needs to know from what could reveal an individual. Privacy is not solved by saying data is confidential; the route from a person’s information to the visible result needs scrutiny.
mavens.tryIt: Choose one AI-assisted report or dashboard that uses people’s data. List the exact audience, the group-level question it answers, and the smallest result that audience needs. Then ask whether a colleague could combine the output with what they already know to infer something sensitive about one person. If the answer might be yes, stop and bring the data owner or privacy lead into the review before sharing it.
mavens.boundary: This is a teaching interpretation of privacy-preserving thinking, not legal or security advice. A workplace review cannot establish a formal privacy guarantee on its own.

concepts.name: Differential privacy
concepts.connection: A formal privacy guarantee limits how much an analysis can reveal about whether any one person's data was included.

concepts.name: Privacy budgets
concepts.connection: Repeated queries consume privacy protection, so disclosure must be managed across the whole analysis.

concepts.name: Aggregate analysis
concepts.connection: Useful group patterns can sometimes be studied without exposing an individual's contribution.

mavens.humanInteraction: People decide which analyses are worth the privacy cost, set acceptable protection and resist interpreting a mathematical guarantee as permission to collect anything. Users still need to know what the guarantee covers and what other information the system releases.
mavens.whyItMattersNow: Organisations want to learn from customer, employee and public data while deploying AI. Differential privacy makes protection testable, but it also reveals the need to manage repeated use instead of treating anonymisation as a one-time label.

mavens.name: Daphne Koller
mavens.about: Daphne Koller is founder and CEO of insitro and remains an adjunct faculty member at Stanford, where her research page describes probabilistic models and machine learning for uncertain, complex domains.
mavens.lesson: When evidence is uncertain, represent alternatives and confidence instead of converting a guess into certainty.
mavens.whyHere: Daphne Koller belongs here because her work makes uncertainty part of the model rather than something to hide after the fact. She founded and leads insitro and remains an adjunct faculty member at Stanford, where her research covers probabilistic models and machine learning for uncertain, complex domains.
contribution: A probabilistic approach does not force one shaky answer to pose as certainty. It keeps alternative explanations and confidence in view when the available evidence does not settle the question.
That is useful wherever AI is asked to advise on a messy situation: a prediction can be helpful while still needing to show what is unclear, variable, or missing.
mavens.move: LAiDIES interpretation: ask an AI system to separate its recommendation from the evidence that makes it tentative. The goal is not to make work indecisive; it is to avoid converting a guess into a fact because the sentence sounds fluent.
mavens.tryIt: Use one live planning question with incomplete information, such as which customer issue to investigate first. Ask the AI for its recommendation, the two strongest alternatives, and the information that would change its answer. Before treating it as a conclusion, make sure the decision-maker can see what the recommendation depends on. If those dependencies remain hidden, keep it as a draft hypothesis.
mavens.boundary: This profile does not say every business decision requires a probabilistic model. It borrows one discipline from work on uncertainty: confidence should be visible when evidence is incomplete.

concepts.name: Probabilistic graphical models
concepts.connection: A model represents dependencies among uncertain variables rather than collapsing them into one unexplained score.

concepts.name: Uncertainty
concepts.connection: Evidence can support several possible explanations with different levels of confidence.

concepts.name: Machine learning for discovery
concepts.connection: Models can prioritise patterns and experiments in complex domains while remaining dependent on real-world validation.

mavens.humanInteraction: A decision-maker asks what alternatives the model considered, how confidence changes with new evidence and which experiment could distinguish competing explanations. AI helps organise uncertainty; the person decides what evidence is strong enough to act on.
mavens.whyItMattersNow: AI is being used in science, medicine and business decisions where certainty is rarely available. Representing alternatives and uncertainty prevents a ranked output from masquerading as a proven cause or guaranteed outcome.

mavens.name: Barbara Liskov
mavens.about: MIT lists Barbara Liskov as an Institute Professor; EECS lists her as Institute Professor post-tenure. CSAIL identifies her as head of the Programming Methodology Group.
mavens.lesson: Put a clear interface around each component so its hidden implementation can change without breaking the people and systems that depend on it.

links.label: Read Barbara Liskov’s MIT EECS profile
Read Barbara Liskov’s MIT CSAIL profile
Watch Barbara Liskov on the power of abstraction

mavens.whyHere: Barbara Liskov belongs here because this profile draws a practical boundary lesson from abstraction: complex systems become more usable when the promise between their parts is clear. MIT identifies her as an Institute Professor and head of the Programming Methodology Group at CSAIL.
contribution: An interface states what one part of a system promises to provide, without forcing every other part to know how it is built. That lets the hidden implementation change without breaking the people and systems that depend on it.
The same idea helps explain why an AI feature is not just a clever model. It needs clear inputs, clear outputs, and clear expectations for the people using it.
mavens.move: LAiDIES interpretation: make the promise at the edge of an AI workflow explicit before arguing about its internal cleverness. A good boundary tells a colleague what to provide, what they will receive, and what remains their responsibility.
mavens.tryIt: Pick one AI-assisted handoff, such as turning call notes into a client follow-up. Write a three-line interface: the approved input, the expected output, and the human who must approve it. Replace the tool with a manual draft or second suitable tool and see whether the next person can follow the same handoff. If the substitution breaks the promise, clarify the interface before scaling the workflow.
mavens.boundary: This is a practical reading of abstraction, not a claim that a short team brief implements Liskov’s technical work. Clear boundaries improve coordination; they do not by themselves prove an AI output is correct.

concepts.name: Abstraction
concepts.connection: A component exposes what others need to use while hiding implementation details that may change.

concepts.name: Substitutability
concepts.connection: A replacement should preserve the promises that dependent users and systems rely on.

concepts.name: Modular systems
concepts.connection: Clear boundaries contain change and make complex technology easier to test and maintain.

mavens.humanInteraction: People rely on an AI service through an interface or contract: accepted inputs, expected outputs, error behaviour and limits. They can change the model behind that boundary only if the replacement still honours the promises made to users and downstream workflows.
mavens.whyItMattersNow: Models and vendors change rapidly. Strong interfaces let organisations upgrade a component without silently changing privacy, output format, quality or business behaviour across every process that depends on it.

mavens.name: Jean Sammet
mavens.about: Jean Sammet was a Computer History Museum Fellow, a COBOL committee member, IBM’s FORMAC development leader, former ACM president and historian of programming languages. She died in 2017.
mavens.lesson: Languages and notation shape who can give precise instructions to a machine; usability is part of computing power.

links.label: Read Jean Sammet’s Computer History Museum profile

mavens.freshness: Historical contribution and destination checked 2 Sep 2026
mavens.whyHere: Jean Sammet belongs here because programming languages decide who can express precise instructions to a computer and how. She served on the COBOL committee, led IBM’s FORMAC development, was an ACM president, and documented programming-language history; she died in 2017.
contribution: A language is more than a set of commands. Its notation makes some actions easy to state, some mistakes easier to see, and some kinds of work more accessible to more people.
That is why the interface for an AI tool matters. A request box, a template, and the words used around them shape what people believe they are allowed to ask the system to do.
mavens.move: LAiDIES interpretation: treat the wording and structure around an AI tool as part of its power, not as decoration. If a capable workflow can only be used by someone who already knows the private jargon, its usable reach is smaller than it looks.
mavens.tryIt: Choose one prompt template your team expects others to reuse. Give it to someone who did not write it and ask them to explain, in their own words, what it will do and what information it needs. If they cannot make a safe, specific request without translating hidden jargon, rewrite the template in the language of the job before adding more instructions.
mavens.boundary: This profile uses Sammet’s work on languages and notation as an interpretive bridge. It does not equate a modern prompt template with a programming language or claim she taught AI prompting.

concepts.name: Programming languages
concepts.connection: A language determines how people can express instructions, data and relationships to a computer.

concepts.name: Symbolic computation
concepts.connection: Systems can manipulate mathematical symbols and structures, not only calculate numeric values.

concepts.name: Usability
concepts.connection: Computing power expands when its notation matches the problems and people meant to use it.

mavens.humanInteraction: Users work through a language chosen by designers, whether code, formulas, menus or natural-language prompts. That language enables some instructions, obscures others and influences who can participate without a specialist translating every step.
mavens.whyItMattersNow: Conversational AI is another attempt to make powerful computation accessible through a more familiar language. Its ease is valuable, but ambiguity remains: natural language broadens access while making precision and verification more important.

mavens.name: Adele Goldberg
mavens.about: Goldberg did early and important work on Smalltalk at Xerox PARC, helped make its object-oriented approach widely known, and later co-founded ParcPlace Systems. The Computer History Museum identifies her as currently deputy chair of the HITS Science Advisory Board.
mavens.lesson: Interfaces do more than decorate a system: they shape what people think a computer can help them do.

links.label: Read Adele Goldberg’s Computer History Museum profile

mavens.freshness: Historical work and current board role checked 2 Sep 2026
mavens.whyHere: Adele Goldberg belongs here because her early Smalltalk work at Xerox PARC helped make an object-oriented approach widely known, and because she shows that an interface changes what people think a computer can help them do. She later co-founded ParcPlace Systems and is identified by the Computer History Museum as deputy chair of the HITS Science Advisory Board.
contribution: A computer interface is not a cosmetic layer placed after the real work. It gives people a way to see possibilities, act on them, and understand the shape of a system.

That is especially relevant to AI. A system may have impressive underlying capability, but its practical effect depends on whether people can tell what it is for, what it needs from them, and how to steer it.
mavens.move: LAiDIES interpretation: judge an AI interface by the work it makes thinkable and doable for a new user, not only by the model behind it. A clearer surface should expand a person’s agency without hiding the limits of the tool.
mavens.tryIt: Choose an AI feature your team says is powerful but rarely uses. Watch one colleague attempt a real task with no coaching and note the first moment they hesitate: what to ask, what the result means, or what to do next. Repair the interface or instruction at that exact moment so the next useful action becomes visible before writing another promotional description of the feature.
mavens.boundary: This is a bounded reading of Goldberg’s contribution to Smalltalk and interfaces. Ease of use does not prove a system is safe, accurate, or appropriate for every task.

concepts.name: Object-oriented programming
concepts.connection: Software can be organised as interacting objects that combine state and behaviour.

concepts.name: Graphical user interfaces
concepts.connection: Visible windows, icons and direct manipulation change how people imagine and control a computer.

concepts.name: Human-computer interaction
concepts.connection: Interface choices shape discoverability, expectations and the kinds of work users attempt.

mavens.humanInteraction: People understand a system through the objects and actions its interface makes visible. AI chat, copilots and creative tools similarly frame what the model appears able to do; the interface can invite useful control or hide consequential automation behind one button.
mavens.whyItMattersNow: AI capability is increasingly mediated by product design rather than exposed as raw models. Interface decisions determine whether users can supply context, inspect sources, revise outputs and understand when the system is acting beyond the task they intended.

mavens.name: Shafi Goldwasser
mavens.about: Goldwasser is RSA Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science at MIT, Professor at UC Berkeley, and part of MIT CSAIL’s Theory of Computation and Cryptography and Information Security groups.
mavens.lesson: Privacy can be designed into a system’s mathematics and protocol—not added later as a promise.

links.label: Read Shafi Goldwasser’s MIT CSAIL profile
Read Shafi Goldwasser at MIT Theory
Read MIT’s Cryptography and Information Security Group

mavens.whyHere: Shafi Goldwasser belongs here because her foundational cryptography work with collaborators introduced probabilistic encryption and zero-knowledge proofs. Those contributions changed security from a reassuring promise into properties that protocols could define and test.
contribution: Goldwasser and Silvio Micali introduced probabilistic encryption, making randomness part of modern cryptographic security; Goldwasser, Micali, and Charles Rackoff introduced zero-knowledge proofs, which can establish a fact without revealing the secret behind it.
Together these ideas make privacy and verifiability design questions. For an AI user, that reframes ‘Do we trust this tool?’ as ‘What can this system prove, and what must it reveal to do so?’
mavens.move: LAiDIES interpretation: turn a security promise into a property that can be demonstrated. Name what must remain secret, what another party needs to verify, and whether the system can establish that fact without exposing the protected material.
mavens.tryIt: Take one workflow where a colleague needs proof of a condition but not the underlying confidential data—for example, confirming that a threshold was met without circulating every employee record. Write the minimum statement they need to verify and the information that must stay hidden. Ask the responsible security or privacy specialist whether an approved aggregate, attestation, or privacy-preserving protocol can prove that statement. If the workflow still reveals the raw records, do not describe it as privacy-preserving merely because access is limited.
mavens.boundary: This is not a cryptography tutorial or a certification that a particular AI product protects data. The profile carries forward the design principle, not a guarantee.

concepts.name: Cryptography
concepts.connection: Cryptographic protocols use mathematical properties to protect information and establish security claims.

concepts.name: Zero-knowledge proofs
concepts.connection: One party can establish that a statement is true without revealing the secret information used to prove it.

concepts.name: Probabilistic encryption
concepts.connection: Randomness prevents encryption from turning the same message into the same predictable ciphertext every time.

mavens.humanInteraction: People need to distinguish a system that asks for trust from one that can demonstrate a property. They choose which facts must be revealed, which can be proved indirectly and which security assumptions remain outside the mathematical guarantee.
mavens.whyItMattersNow: AI services increasingly handle identity, proprietary data and sensitive computation. Cryptographic methods can reduce unnecessary disclosure and support verifiable claims, but only when the whole product preserves the assumptions the protocol requires.

mavens.name: Lynn Conway
mavens.about: Conway was a University of Michigan Professor Emerita whose work with Carver Mead helped establish scalable VLSI design methodology. She died in June 2024; this card uses historical wording, not a present-tense current role.
mavens.lesson: Good design rules let more people build complex technology without each person having to rediscover every constraint.

links.label: Read Lynn Conway’s University of Michigan archive
Read the University of Michigan tribute

mavens.freshness: Historical contribution and death record checked 2 Sep 2026
mavens.whyHere: Lynn Conway belongs here because her work with Carver Mead helped establish scalable VLSI design methodology: rules that let many people design intricate chips without each person rediscovering every physical constraint. She was University of Michigan Professor Emerita and died in June 2024.
contribution: Complex technology becomes buildable at scale when a shared method absorbs recurring constraints into usable rules. The method does not remove the underlying complexity; it gives more people a dependable way to work with it.

That is a useful lens for AI adoption. Teams need a repeatable way to choose a task, provide context, review an output, and learn from mistakes—rather than relying on one expert to improvise every time.
mavens.move: LAiDIES interpretation: turn the parts of an AI workflow people repeatedly have to rediscover into a simple, visible method. The aim is to widen capable participation while keeping the important constraints in view.
mavens.tryIt: Find one AI task that only one confident colleague currently performs. Document the smallest repeatable method: the approved use case, the input they gather, the review they perform, and the place they record a correction. Give it to a second person and note every hidden constraint they have to guess. Turn those constraints into visible rules before calling the workflow ready to scale.
mavens.boundary: This is an analogy from scalable chip-design methodology, not a claim that AI work follows the same technical rules. A documented process still needs human judgement and revision.

concepts.name: VLSI design
concepts.connection: Very-large-scale integration places many components on a chip and requires methods for managing their complexity.

concepts.name: Design rules
concepts.connection: Shared abstractions let designers work within manufacturing constraints without rediscovering every physical detail.

concepts.name: Democratising technical creation
concepts.connection: Tools, notation and education can widen who is able to design advanced systems.

mavens.humanInteraction: People build complex technology by working through layers of trusted rules and tools. AI users do the same when they combine models, prompts and services; they need to know which constraints are safely abstracted and which decisions remain theirs.
mavens.whyItMattersNow: Modern AI depends on specialised chips, while AI tools themselves promise to widen technical creation. Conway's work shows that access grows when complexity is organised into teachable interfaces—not when expertise is dismissed or hidden.

trailblazers.name: Mira Murati
trailblazers.about: Murati is co-founder and CEO of Thinking Machines Lab.
trailblazers.lesson: A powerful model becomes more useful when people can inspect, adapt, and steer it for the work they actually need done.

links.label: Read Thinking Machines Lab’s NVIDIA partnership
Follow Thinking Machines Lab on X

trailblazers.whyHere: Mira Murati belongs here because she is co-founder and CEO of Thinking Machines Lab, a current AI-building role with a direct public route into the organisation’s work. Her place in this wing is about present-day AI being built, not a claim that she represents a complete philosophy of AI.
contribution: As co-founder and CEO of Thinking Machines Lab, Murati is building an AI organisation rather than commenting from the sidelines. That present-day role opens a practical question: how can people adapt and steer advanced systems for the work they actually need done?
As a LAiDIES teaching interpretation, it asks whether a system can be inspected and steered enough for the real job at hand, rather than being treated as a black-box answer machine.
trailblazers.move: LAiDIES interpretation: ask for the handles you need to direct and inspect an AI system in your own work. A capable model is more useful when the person accountable for the outcome can see what to adjust and what to check.
trailblazers.tryIt: Take one AI task where the first answer is too generic, such as drafting a project brief. List the three choices a human owner needs to steer: audience, source material, and success criteria. Change one choice at a time and compare what the system does. If the output does not respond predictably, add the missing context or choose a workflow with clearer control before using it for a decision.
trailblazers.boundary: This profile does not assign Murati a personal philosophy she has not stated. Its steering lesson is LAiDIES' interpretation of the work of building an AI organisation.

concepts.name: Human-AI collaboration
concepts.connection: A useful system gives people ways to direct, inspect and revise what the model contributes.

concepts.name: Steerability
concepts.connection: Users need controls that make behaviour respond predictably to goals, context and correction.

concepts.name: Customisation
concepts.connection: A general model becomes a work tool when it can incorporate the user's domain, constraints and feedback without losing safety boundaries.

trailblazers.humanInteraction: People move from receiving a generic answer to shaping a working partner: they provide context, compare alternatives, correct behaviour and decide what remains under human control. Collaboration requires observable handles, not simply a friendlier tone.
trailblazers.whyItMattersNow: Advanced models are becoming components in products and workflows rather than isolated chat windows. The quality of steering, adaptation and review will determine whether those systems support professional judgement or merely automate plausible output at greater scale.

trailblazers.name: Daniela Amodei
trailblazers.about: Amodei is President and Co-Founder of Anthropic, a Public Benefit Corporation developing and deploying AI systems.
trailblazers.lesson: Research does not become dependable technology by itself: operations, governance, product choices, and safety practices determine what reaches people.

links.label: Watch Daniela Amodei on building AI responsibly

trailblazers.whyHere: Daniela Amodei belongs here because she is President and Co-Founder of Anthropic, a Public Benefit Corporation developing and deploying AI systems. This profile uses that verified organisational role to make the operating, governance, and product layer of AI visible.
contribution: AI does not arrive in the world solely as a model. It is delivered through teams, decisions, rules, and product experiences that determine who can use it, how it is managed, and what happens when something goes wrong.
That organisational layer matters to a nontechnical user because the dependable use of AI depends on more than the apparent quality of one response.
trailblazers.move: LAiDIES interpretation: when assessing an AI tool, look past the demo to the organisation around it. Ask who owns the workflow, how concerns are handled, and what practical choices make the technology dependable for real people.
trailblazers.tryIt: Choose one AI feature your team is considering introducing. Make a short operating map with a named owner, the people affected, the decision it supports, and the route for reporting a failure. Walk one plausible failure through the map. If nobody has authority to stop, investigate, and change the workflow, keep the proposal in discovery rather than calling it ready.
trailblazers.boundary: This profile does not claim that Anthropic’s public materials settle every question about responsible AI. It uses Amodei’s verified role to make the organisational layer of deployment visible.

concepts.name: AI operations
concepts.connection: Research becomes a dependable service through staffing, infrastructure, incident response and repeatable operating processes.

concepts.name: Governance
concepts.connection: Organisational authority determines who can approve, stop, investigate and change an AI system.

concepts.name: Safety as a system
concepts.connection: Technical testing, policy, product choices and deployment controls must work together rather than live in separate documents.

trailblazers.humanInteraction: Customers and employees encounter not only a model but the organisation operating it. They depend on escalation routes, transparent limits, support, monitoring and leadership decisions when the system behaves unexpectedly.
trailblazers.whyItMattersNow: Companies are embedding frontier models into consequential products. Reliability depends on whether the organisation can translate research findings into product restrictions, operational practice and accountable decisions under commercial pressure.

trailblazers.name: Lila Ibrahim
trailblazers.about: Ibrahim is Chief Operating Officer of Google DeepMind and co-chair of its Responsibility and Safety Council.
trailblazers.lesson: When AI moves from a lab into public systems, responsibility has to be operational: create the review forum, bring in affected expertise, and keep improving it from feedback.

links.label: Read Google DeepMind’s Responsibility & Safety work
Read about Google DeepMind’s India partnerships

trailblazers.whyHere: Lila Ibrahim belongs here because she is Chief Operating Officer of Google DeepMind and co-chair of its Responsibility and Safety Council. Those verified roles make visible a problem beyond any single experiment: how research programmes acquire the people, checkpoints, and operating discipline needed to learn at scale.
contribution: Google DeepMind says its Responsibility and Safety Council evaluates research, projects, and collaborations against the organisation’s AI Principles, working with research and product teams on high-impact work.

Ibrahim’s operating and council roles make institutional governance visible: responsibility needs a standing forum, defined authority, relevant expertise, and a route for evidence to change a decision. The portfolio method below is LAiDIES’ workplace transfer from that structure, not a description of Google DeepMind’s internal process.
trailblazers.move: LAiDIES interpretation: manage research as a sequence of answerable questions, not a queue of exciting possibilities. Give each question an owner, the evidence needed to advance it, a responsibility checkpoint, and a reason to stop. Scale comes from a system that preserves what teams learn, not from running more experiments at once.
trailblazers.tryIt: Take three AI experiments your organisation is considering and place each in one stage: explore, evaluate, or prepare for use. For each, name the question being tested, the evidence required to move forward, the specialist or affected perspective still missing, and the stop condition. Ask the portfolio owner to justify the next unit of time for each item. Pause anything that has momentum but no answerable question or exit criterion.
trailblazers.boundary: This profile does not represent every Google DeepMind policy or outcome. It draws a workplace practice from Ibrahim’s verified operational and responsibility roles.

concepts.name: Responsible scaling
concepts.connection: Controls and oversight must grow as a system's capability, reach and consequence grow.

concepts.name: Institutional governance
concepts.connection: Standing forums, defined authority and diverse expertise make responsibility operable.

concepts.name: Feedback loops
concepts.connection: Deployment reveals new evidence that should change testing, policy and design rather than disappear into support queues.

trailblazers.humanInteraction: People affected by AI need routes to report failure, contribute expertise and trigger a real organisational response. Operators decide who sits at the review table and whether feedback can alter a model, product or deployment decision.
trailblazers.whyItMattersNow: AI is moving from research environments into education, science, healthcare and public infrastructure. Responsibility cannot remain a principle on an about page; it needs owners, meetings, evidence and the power to change what ships.

trailblazers.name: Fidji Simo
trailblazers.about: Simo is CEO of Applications at OpenAI.
trailblazers.lesson: Deployment is not the last step after a model works; it is the operating system that connects products, teams, and economic opportunity.

links.label: Read Fidji Simo on expanding economic opportunity with AI

trailblazers.whyHere: Fidji Simo belongs here because she is CEO of Applications at OpenAI, a role focused on turning AI capabilities into products people can use. Her place in this wing asks a practical deployment question: what has to be true before a promising system belongs in someone's real workflow?
contribution: LAiDIES interpretation: a model working in a test setting is not the same thing as a product working for people. An application connects technical capability to a task, a team, and a workflow where value or harm can show up.
That makes deployment a live design problem: whether the product helps a person complete meaningful work, not merely whether the underlying system can produce an answer.
trailblazers.move: LAiDIES interpretation: evaluate AI use where it lands—in the workflow, not at the demo. Ask what job the application changes, who carries the new work around it, and what evidence would show that it is helping rather than adding friction.
trailblazers.tryIt: Choose one AI feature your team already has access to and follow one real piece of work from input to final handoff. Mark every place a person has to reformat, correct, re-enter, explain, or chase the output. Compare the work removed with the work shifted downstream. Repair the worst handoff before measuring adoption by logins or usage counts.
trailblazers.boundary: This is a LAiDIES interpretation of product deployment, not a biography of Simo or a statement of OpenAI strategy. The available evidence does not support broader claims about her personal philosophy.

concepts.name: AI deployment
concepts.connection: A model reaches people through products, permissions, pricing, distribution and support systems.

concepts.name: Productisation
concepts.connection: Capability becomes usable when it is shaped around a real task, interface and operating context.

concepts.name: Economic access
concepts.connection: Who can adopt a technology depends on cost, skills, infrastructure and how benefits are distributed.

trailblazers.humanInteraction: Users experience AI through the decisions surrounding the model: where it appears, what it can access, which actions it may take and what help exists when it fails. Adoption is shaped as much by those product choices as by benchmark performance.
trailblazers.whyItMattersNow: AI companies are racing to move models into everyday applications and organisations. Deployment choices determine who gains practical capability, who absorbs transition costs and whether a promising demonstration becomes dependable work.

trailblazers.name: Chelsea Finn
trailblazers.about: Finn is Assistant Professor of Computer Science and Electrical Engineering at Stanford University and co-founder of Physical Intelligence (π).
trailblazers.lesson: A robot’s competence must be tested on the feedback its actions create in new conditions—not only on whether it can copy a demonstration.
trailblazers.whyHere: Chelsea Finn belongs here because she is a Stanford professor in Computer Science and Electrical Engineering and co-founder of Physical Intelligence. Her work makes embodied AI concrete: a robot has to perform multi-stage tasks in physical conditions that do not stay identical to a prepared demonstration.
contribution: Robotic intelligence is judged through action in a physical environment, including tasks with several connected stages rather than one isolated motor skill.

That offers a useful warning for any AI system that influences an ongoing process. A system can look convincing on a static sample yet fail when its output changes the next step for a customer, colleague, or machine.
trailblazers.move: LAiDIES interpretation: test an AI-assisted workflow after its output meets the next person or condition, not only at the moment it is generated. The relevant question is whether the work still holds when reality responds.
trailblazers.tryIt: Pick an AI-produced handoff, such as a drafted customer reply or triaged support ticket, and follow five examples to the next actual outcome. Note what the recipient did, what needed correction, and whether the output created a new problem downstream. Revise the workflow using that feedback instead of judging it from a single polished first screen.
trailblazers.boundary: This profile uses embodied-AI thinking as a transfer lens; it does not say office workflows are robots. The point is the feedback loop, not a literal comparison.

concepts.name: Embodied AI
concepts.connection: An embodied system learns and acts through a physical environment where mistakes change the next situation.

concepts.name: Imitation and reinforcement learning
concepts.connection: Robots can learn from demonstrations and feedback, but must generalise beyond the exact examples shown.

concepts.name: Adaptation
concepts.connection: A capable system adjusts to new objects, tasks and conditions rather than replaying a memorised routine.

trailblazers.humanInteraction: People demonstrate tasks, define rewards, supervise trials and decide which failures are safe enough for learning. Because a robot's output is an action, oversight must account for physical consequences and recovery—not only whether a sentence looks correct.
trailblazers.whyItMattersNow: AI is moving from screens into warehouses, laboratories and homes. Real-world variation makes impressive demonstrations insufficient; organisations need tests that reveal how the system responds when the environment stops matching the training example.

trailblazers.name: Amanda Askell
trailblazers.about: Askell leads Anthropic’s Character work and is the primary author of Claude’s Constitution.
trailblazers.lesson: Model character is not a vibes setting: state the intended values, explain their trade-offs, and test whether behaviour still follows them under pressure.

links.label: Watch Amanda Askell answer questions about Claude’s character

trailblazers.whyHere: Amanda Askell belongs here because she leads Anthropic’s Character work and is the primary author of Claude’s Constitution. Her work makes visible that model behaviour is shaped by stated values, trade-offs, and testing—not by an unexplained personality setting.
contribution: A model’s character is a set of intended behavioural commitments. To be meaningful, those commitments have to be written down clearly enough to examine, and tested where the pressures and trade-offs are real.
That matters because a tool can sound helpful and still behave inconsistently when a request is ambiguous, urgent, or in tension with another value.
trailblazers.move: LAiDIES interpretation: when a team says it wants an AI assistant to be helpful, careful, or on-brand, turn those adjectives into visible choices and test cases. Values that never affect a difficult response are merely a mood board.
trailblazers.tryIt: Take one internal AI assistant or prompt guide and name two values it is meant to protect, such as accuracy and a respectful tone. Create three difficult-but-real requests where those values could pull in different directions, then review the responses with the person accountable for the workflow. If the team cannot explain why one response should be preferred, make the intended trade-off explicit before relying on the assistant in higher-stakes work.
trailblazers.boundary: This profile does not claim that every AI team should use Claude’s Constitution or that a written set of values guarantees good behaviour. It borrows the practice of making behavioural commitments inspectable and testable.

concepts.name: AI alignment
concepts.connection: A system's behaviour is shaped toward intended goals and constraints, while conflicts among those aims must be made explicit.

concepts.name: Model character
concepts.connection: Consistent behavioural tendencies affect how a model communicates, refuses and handles uncertainty.

concepts.name: Constitutional approaches
concepts.connection: Written principles can guide training and critique, but their interpretation and trade-offs still need evaluation.

trailblazers.humanInteraction: People encounter alignment through everyday behaviour: what the model will help with, how it explains a refusal, whether it admits uncertainty and how it responds when instructions conflict. Users can test those behaviours with difficult cases instead of judging character from a friendly first exchange.
trailblazers.whyItMattersNow: General-purpose assistants increasingly mediate writing, analysis and decisions. The values embedded in their behaviour affect millions of small interactions, making explicit principles, trade-offs and adversarial testing practical product concerns rather than abstract philosophy.

trailblazers.whyHere: Allie K. Miller belongs here because her work is centred on practical AI adoption: she is an AI business leader, adviser, investor, and international speaker, and was formerly AWS’s Global Head of Machine Learning for Startups and Venture Capital. Her value to this wing is the bridge from a tool demonstration to a business workflow that has to work for actual people.
contribution: Using AI once is not the same as adopting it. Adoption starts with a specific business decision or task, a definition of what improvement looks like, and a redesign of the surrounding work so people can actually use the result.
That reframes success away from novelty or usage counts. The relevant evidence is whether the workflow has become more useful, reliable, or manageable for the people doing the work.
trailblazers.move: LAiDIES interpretation: begin with the decision you want to improve, then choose the AI use that can change it and the measure that can prove it. Treat the tool as one part of a workflow, not the workflow itself.
trailblazers.tryIt: Choose one recurring decision, such as which leads need follow-up this week, rather than starting with a tool. Define one success measure—fewer missed leads, faster preparation, or better-qualified handoffs—then run a two-week trial with a named human owner. Compare the result with the starting baseline and ask the people in the workflow where rework moved. Change the process around the tool before expanding it if the promised improvement did not appear.
trailblazers.boundary: This profile does not claim that Miller endorses this exact adoption method or that every task needs AI. The lesson is a LAiDIES interpretation of practical adoption, bounded by a real business measure and human review.

concepts.name: AI adoption
concepts.connection: Adoption means changing a real workflow and its outcomes, not accumulating tool accounts or isolated demos.

concepts.name: Workflow redesign
concepts.connection: The task, handoffs, data and human decisions around the model determine whether capability becomes useful work.

concepts.name: Measurement and change management
concepts.connection: Teams need a baseline, success measure, owner and feedback from the people expected to use the system.

trailblazers.humanInteraction: People choose a real decision or bottleneck, test where AI can change it and compare the new workflow with the old one. They report hidden rework, confusion and exceptions instead of allowing usage statistics to stand in for usefulness.
trailblazers.whyItMattersNow: Organisations are under pressure to show AI adoption quickly. Starting from business outcomes protects them from scaling a fashionable tool that adds review work, weakens accountability or solves a problem employees did not actually have.
